extraction.name: SeamlessM4T
extraction.description: SeamlessM4T (Massively Multilingual & Multimodal Machine Translation) is a single unified model that supports speech-to-speech translation, speech-to-text translation, text-to-speech translation, text-to-text translation, and automatic speech recognition for up to 100 languages. It was built using 1 million hours of open speech audio data for self-supervised speech representations (w2v-BERT 2.0), and a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations called SeamlessAlign (470,000 hours). Combined with human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data (totaling 406,000 hours), it is the first multilingual system capable of translating from and into English for both speech and text.
extraction.creator: Seamless Communication, Meta AI
extraction.inLanguage: Multiple (up to 100 languages including English, Arabic, Bengali, Catalan, Czech, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin Chinese, Dutch, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, Swahili, Tagalog, Tamil, Telugu, Thai, Turkish, Ukrainian, Urdu, Vietnamese, and others)
extraction.citeAs: Seamless Communication et al., SeamlessM4T: Massively Multilingual & Multimodal Machine Translation, arXiv:2308.11596v3, 2023.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected through multiple approaches: (1) 1 million hours of open speech audio data from publicly available crawled web data for unsupervised pre-training of w2v-BERT 2.0; (2) parallel data mining using SONAR embeddings to create SeamlessAlign, a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations totaling 470,000 hours from 4 million hours of raw audio; (3) human-labeled S2TT and ASR data from open-source datasets; (4) pseudo-labeled data generated by applying NLLB-200-3.3B to ASR transcriptions. The text side relied on the same dataset deployed in NLLB. Audio was deduplicated, downloaded, resampled at 16KHz, and filtered using an audio event detection model.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Some samples from the CVSS evaluation data were missing in 8 out of 21 languages: Catalan, German, Estonian, French, Italian, Mongolian, Persian, and Portuguese. For Maltese, only a small amount of raw audio was available, limiting mined speech alignments. Some languages had zero-shot coverage due to absence of supervised labeled data.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw audio originated from a publicly available repository of crawled web data totaling 4 million hours. Text data was drawn from the NLLB dataset (same data sources, cleaning, and filtering steps). Human-labeled speech data came from open-source corpora including VoxLingua107, FLEURS, VAANI, IIITH, KENCORPUS, CoVoST, mTEDx, and others. Additional open-source T2TT datasets not included in NLLB were also incorporated for Modern Standard Arabic, Mandarin Chinese, French, Russian, and Spanish.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Speech audio files were deduplicated by URL, downloaded, and resampled at 16KHz. Non-speech data was filtered using a bespoke audio event detection (AED) model. Audio was segmented using Voice Activity Detection (VAD) with an over-segmentation strategy (creating overlapping splits, roughly octupling the number of potential segments). Speech language identification (LID) was applied per segment. Text was processed using the same pipeline as NLLB with the Stopes library. A toxicity filter was applied to remove pairs with toxicity imbalance. Length filtering removed utterances shorter than 0.1s or longer than 50s, and text longer than 250 sub-words. Pairs with more than 20% emojis, 50% punctuations, or 50% spaces were also removed. For S2ST data, pseudo-labeling was performed using multilingual text-to-unit (T2U) models to convert text into discrete acoustic units.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Audio preprocessing: deduplication of URLs, downloading, resampling at 16KHz, filtering non-speech with AED model, VAD-based segmentation with over-segmentation, LID filtering (rejecting 8% of data below per-language threshold to improve F1 by ~3%). Text preprocessing: same cleaning and filtering as NLLB using Stopes library. For human-labeled data: removal of special tokens (<silence>, <no-speech>), length filtering (max 100 sub-word tokens, max text-to-audio ratio of 5 sub-words/second). For mined data: top 400 hours per X-eng direction and top 200 hours per eng-X direction based on SONAR alignment scores were selected. A 256K SentencePiece vocabulary was retrained on NLLB data with forced inclusion of top 5000 Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, and Japanese kanji characters.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human evaluation used two protocols: (1) XSTS (Cross-lingual Semantic Textual Similarity) protocol to assess translation quality in terms of semantic meaning preservation for S2TT and S2ST tasks. Annotators evaluated source-target audio/text pairs on a 1-5 scale. 3 annotators per item; if disagreement of 2+ points, 2 additional annotators were added (total 5). Median score per sentence was taken. A cross-lingual calibration set was used for inter-language comparison. (2) MOS (Mean Opinion Score) protocol to evaluate naturalness, sound quality, and clarity of speech for S2ST. Annotators provided Likert scores (1-5) for three questions about clarity, sound quality, and naturalness. 3 annotators per item for most languages; some languages had only 1 annotator per item. Human evaluation of toxicity detection was also performed to identify true positives and false positives among automatically detected toxic outputs.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For XSTS: median score over annotators was taken per sentence for robustness. In cases of disagreement (score difference of 2+), 2 additional annotators were consulted. Language-level scores were calibrated using a cross-lingual calibration set and 'moderated calibration' methodology to reduce annotator biases. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate language score uncertainty. For MOS: median of annotator scores collected per item; no calibration performed. Blaser 2.0 correlation with XSTS was analyzed, showing superior correlation compared to ASR-BLEU and BLEU metrics. Annotator crews sufficiently out of calibration could be identified and excluded.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 annotators per item for XSTS (up to 5 in cases of disagreement of 2+ points); 3 annotators per item for MOS for most languages, with some languages receiving scores from only 1 annotator per item.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: ETOX (word-list based toxicity detection using Toxicity-200 word lists) for automatic toxicity detection; Whisper-Medium and Whisper-Large-v2 for ASR transcription in ASR-BLEU and ASR-ETOX metrics; Blaser 2.0 (supervised and unsupervised versions) for automatic quality estimation; SONAR speech and text encoders for embedding-based mining and evaluation; FAISS library for large-scale similarity search; Silero VAD for voice activity detection; LID100 (ECAPA-TDNN based) for speech language identification; MMS-TTS for speech synthesis in bias evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: All contributions are open-sourced at https://github.com/facebookresearch/seamless_communication, including model weights for SeamlessM4T-Large (2.3B parameters) and SeamlessM4T-Medium (1.2B parameters), inference code, fine-tuning recipes powered by Fairseq2, metadata to recreate the unfiltered 470,000 hours of SeamlessAlign, Stopes-based pipelines, and SONAR encoders. The model is released under CC-BY-NC 4.0 license. The model is described as a research model not released for production deployment. Future iterations are planned to scale mining to all 100 languages.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The training data was mined from publicly available sources on the web. Although heavy data cleaning was invested, personally identifiable information may not be entirely eliminated. Speaker gender information is present in Fleurs recordings (gender-matched pairings were made 53% of the time). Gender attributes are analyzed in bias evaluations using Multilingual HolisticBias dataset covering demographic axes including ability, race/ethnicity, gender/sex, nationality, religion, sexual orientation, socioeconomic class, age, body type, cultural, characteristics, and political ideologies.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: SeamlessM4T could augment world-readiness by lowering barriers in cross-lingual communication, supporting those with accessibility needs (blind or visually impaired individuals, those without reading/writing skills), and helping communities with script variance or endangered languages. However, access could make groups with lower digital literacy more vulnerable to misinformation or online scams if misappropriated. The system may perform differently across user demographics based on gender, race, accent, or language. The authors urge that SeamlessM4T-fueled applications be viewed as augmentation tools rather than replacements for human interpreters, especially in high-stakes legal or medical contexts.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Gender bias: SeamlessM4T-Large exhibits an average preference of ~10% towards translating to masculine forms when no gender information is available in the source. Using feminine form as source leads to lower quality English translations compared to masculine counterpart (~3% lack of robustness against gender inflection). Masculine lexical representation is predominant in most training and evaluation datasets (EuroParl, Flores, Fleurs, CoVoST 2, LibriSpeech, MultilingualLibriSpeech, and mined SeamlessAlign data). Cultural, body type, socioeconomic class, and religion axes are most sensitive to quality disruptions in bias evaluation. Some languages show toxicity concentrated in specific demographic axes (e.g., Bengali 80% socio-economic status, Nyanja 66% characteristics, Kyrgyz 94% cultural).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The model is trained on general domain data and not intended for domain-specific inputs (medical, legal). Not intended for long-form translation as it was trained on short text and speech inputs. SeamlessM4T translations cannot be used as certified translations. Word list-based toxicity detection (ETOX) tends to over-detect terms only toxic in specific contexts and relies on precise tokenization, which is harder for non-segmenting or highly agglutinative languages. ASR before lexical matching adds error sources leading to false negatives, particularly for non-English languages. Gender detection using noun lists does not guarantee generalizability to all noun sets. Fleurs test set is limited to a maximum of 3 speakers per language, introducing potential speaker diversity bias. Some languages (Igbo, Burmese, Nepali, Assamese) have issues with segmentation and toxicity word list consistencies leading to over-detection and were excluded from toxicity analysis. ASR performance may vary based on gender, race, accent, or language.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primary use cases: research in speech and text translation including ASR (96 languages), S2ST (100 source to 35 target speech languages), S2TT (100 source speech to 95 target text languages), T2ST (95 source text to 35 target speech languages), T2TT (95 source text to 95 target text languages), and TTS (36 languages). Intended for Training, Testing, and Fine-tuning by researchers and machine translation research community. Not intended for production deployment, domain-specific inputs, long-form translation, or certified translations.
